Summary returned: I didn't find any r/lovable Reddit threads in these results. The matches are mostly vendor pages from freelancers and agencies that sell Lovable rescue work, so treat their pricing and claims as marketing.
- Typical costs: One agency guide says freelance Lovable developers typically charge $50-150/hour or $5,000-$15,000 per project; agencies run $13,000-$25,000 for a full production build.
- Signs you need help: The same guide lists the same bug reappearing after three or more fix attempts, credit usage climbing without visible progress, a security scan flagging issues you don't know how to resolve as warning signs.
- Where to look for help: One guide suggests posting in the Lovable Discord community, where builders and freelancers who specialize in Lovable projects are active, and notes this is peer-to-peer rather than an official hiring channel.
- Support limits: A different guide says that a broken form, a layout issue, an integration that fails silently, or a feature that isn't behaving as intended falls outside Lovable support's scope, so a ticket won't fix the app's code.
- Staying on Lovable: An independent-looking developer's note argues that most founders who ask about alternatives are not actually stuck - they are frustrated. It suggests rescue spending makes sense once you have real users and revenue, or have regulated data.

Summary returned: Two separate episodes. 1. CVE-2025-48757 (2025): misconfigured RLS in user-built apps. A security researcher scanned 1,645 applications from Lovable's own showcase and found 170 of them (10.3%) had critical RLS failures. Attackers needed no login: the public anon_key embedded in the client allowed direct queries to Supabase. Exposed data included contact details, payment and subscription status, and API keys. Severity scores differ (CVSS 8.26 in some, 9.3 in others). 2. April 2026 platform bug reported by @weezerOSINT: a backend regression (BOLA-type) active Feb 3 to Apr 20, 2026, meant anyone with a link to a public Lovable project could read chat history and source code. Bastion's write-up claims broader scope (projects created before November 2025) - treat cautiously. A February 2026 incident exposed 18,697 user records in a featured app, which one source attributes to an inverted authentication check. Several results are vendor marketing pages.
